# Enemies should be aware of the wrap around

## Problem statement

Enemies are currently "wrap-blind": aimed shots always fire a straight line at
the player's raw position (never crossing a screen edge), and enemy movement is
bounded or clamped to the arena, so no enemy ever flies over a screen edge the
way the player ship, asteroids, bullets and the raider patrol already do. The
playfield seam is therefore one-directional — only the player's shots and the
player can cross it — letting the player camp the edges with impunity. Enemy
behaviour should be wrap-aware by default — firing across the seam to reach the
player and flying over the edges — controlled by a per-enemy parameter so a
small set of classic arcade archetypes (Space Invaders march, Centipede) keeps
its bounded, wall-respecting behaviour.

## Users

- **Players** — enemy shots can now arrive from anywhere, including from
  "off-screen" across the seam, so camping a screen edge is no longer a safe
  position. Most enemies occupy the whole wrap-around world rather than a
  bounded box, while the classic set pieces (Space Invaders, Centipede) stay
  recognisible.
- **AI agents / human developers** — one unambiguous data-driven per-archetype
  parameter (`wrapAware`, default `true`) that the game and every gym read
  through the same shared seams, so game↔gym parity is preserved by
  construction and tuning an archetype is a one-field change.

### Example user stories

- As a **player**, I want enemies to fire at me across the screen edge, so that
  hiding against an edge is no longer a guaranteed safe position and shots can
  arrive from the seam exactly like my own wrapped bullets.
- As a **player**, I want most enemies to fly over a screen edge and reappear on
  the opposite side, so the whole wrapped playfield — not a bounded box — is
  part of the arena.
- As a **player**, I want the Space Invaders block and the Centipede to keep
  their classic behaviour (reversing at the walls / weaving within the arena),
  so those recognisable set pieces remain intact.
- As a **developer**, I want a single data-driven `wrapAware` parameter per
  archetype (default: aware) that behaves identically in the game and every
  gym, so enabling or disabling seam-awareness is a one-field change with no
  divergent copies.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **Parameter** — Each enemy archetype carries a data-driven boolean
   `wrapAware` (or equivalently named) parameter, defaulting to `true`, wired
   through the existing `EnemyConfig` pipeline so it is visible and editable in
   the enemy editor panel. The `march` (Space Invaders) and `centipede` seed
   configs set it to `false`.
2. **Seam-aware aimed fire** — Aimed shots (Scout, march and the raider's
   aimed fire — every archetype routed through the aimed-shot method) fire
   along the shortest wrapped path to the player: when the direct line is
   longer than the wrap-around route, the shot leaves one edge and arrives from
   the opposite edge (enemy bullets already wrap; AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0). An
   enemy with `wrapAware: false` keeps the current direct aim.
3. **Wrap-aware movement** — Wrap-aware enemy motion (dive, chase, orbit,
   drift, roam, hold-and-move, etc.) that would carry the enemy off-screen
   wraps to the opposite edge (matching the player/asteroid four-edge wrap
   model) instead of being clamped. Non-aware archetypes (`march`,
   `centipede`) are unchanged: march reverses and drops at the arena edge;
   centipede weaves within bounds.
4. **Gym ↔ game parity** — The behaviour is implemented once in the shared
   core (`src/scenes/core/`) and exercised by the affected gym scene(s) and
   `PlayScene` in the same change, so the repo-wide duplicate-body / parity
   guards stay green.
5. **Testing, validation & docs** — Unit tests cover: seam-aware aim angle for
   wrap-aware enemies vs. direct aim for non-aware enemies; position wrapping
   on crossing each edge for wrap-aware motion; config default / CSV wiring
   including the `march` / `centipede` exclusions. The affected documentation
   (`docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` and any config-format docs) is
   updated to reflect the change. The full project test suite passes with the
   new changes.

## Constraints

- Do not change the bullet wrap model itself — enemy bullets already wrap and
  expire by lifetime (AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0); this item changes launch direction
  and enemy movement only.
- Exclusions are an explicit seed-config list: only `march` and `centipede`
  default to non-aware. During planning, any other archetype whose classic
  design requires wall interaction belongs in the exclusion list, recorded as a
  code comment and a documented divergence per the gym↔game parity convention
  (AH-0MUGZDTFX004RBD1).
- Implement through the shared core (`src/scenes/core/`), never a divergent
  copy, so the game and every gym run the same code.
- Out of scope: boss behaviours, player ship, minerals, drops, and the bullet
  wrap model itself.
- Written in UK English per repo convention.

## Existing state

- Enemy aimed fire: `Scout.tryFireAimedBullet` computes
  `heading = atan2(target.y - y, target.x - x)` on **raw** positions with no
  seam consideration — the same aimed-shot method is reused for march and
  raider via `ENEMY_FIRE_METHODS` (`src/entities/enemyFire.ts`).
- Enemy bullets: wrap all four screen edges and expire by lifetime
  (AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0; shared bullet path in `src/entities/PlayerBullet.ts`).
- Enemy movement: bounded. Ghost/Grunt clamp to `GAME_WIDTH`/`GAME_HEIGHT`;
  march reverses and drops at arena bounds (`src/scenes/core/marchFormation.ts`:
  `computeMarchBounds` / `advanceMarch`); centipede weaves within bounds;
  formation drift pushes rightward.
- Wrap model to match: player ship and `Asteroid.updatePosition` four-edge
  wrap; `Raider` patrol already wraps; `LaneTraffic` wraps horizontally.
- Enemies are data-driven: `EnemyConfig` (`src/core/configTypes.ts`) + seed
  defaults (`src/core/configDefaults.ts`) + CSV (`src/data/enemy-configs.csv`)
  + enemy editor panel + gym editor.

## Desired change

1. Add the boolean parameter to `EnemyConfig` (`wrapAware`), seed default
   `true`; set `march` and `centipede` to `false`.
2. Seam-aware aim: for wrap-aware entities, compute the player delta along the
   shortest wrapped path before `atan2` in the shared aimed-fire seam; used by
   Scout / march / raider aimed fire (and any other archetype sharing the
   aimed-shot method).
3. Shared post-motion edge wrap: in the shared scene entity loop (game +
   gyms), wrap each wrap-aware enemy's position when it crosses an edge; gate
   on the flag so non-aware archetypes are untouched.
4. Verify per-archetype that nothing breaks (divers mid-dive, chasers,
   orbiters, swarm, formation drift) and adjust tests.
5. Update key docs (`docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md`; config-format
   docs if they enumerate fields).

## Key Files

- `src/core/configTypes.ts` — add `wrapAware?: boolean` to `EnemyConfig`.
- `src/core/configDefaults.ts` — seed defaults: `true` for most archetypes;
  `false` for `march` and `centipede`.
- `src/data/enemy-configs.csv` — new `wrapAware` column entries (if the CSV
  persists the field).
- `src/entities/enemyFire.ts` + aimed-fire call sites (`Scout.tryFireAimedBullet`,
  march, `Raider`) — seam-aware aim.
- `src/entities/BaseEnemy.ts` — expose the flag and any shared seam support.
- `src/scenes/core/` — shared post-motion wrap (CombatCoreScene / CombatScene
  shared entity loop, alongside the `enemyTargeting.ts` seams).
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts` + affected gym scenes
  (`GymFodderEnemies`, `GymCentipede`, …) — parity exercises.
- `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` — document the parameter and the
  exclusions.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Risk: gameplay feel** — seam-aware aimed fire lets shots come from
  unexpected directions; mitigated by limiting the change to aimed shots
  (radial/spread remain direction-symmetric) and excluding the classic
  archetypes.
- **Risk: wrap × state-machine interaction** — a post-motion wrap applied to
  every wrap-aware archetype could interact with steering that seeks the player
  or with dive/common state machines near the seam (oscillation). Mitigation:
  per-archetype verification during planning and dedicated unit tests at the
  seam.
- **Risk: formation-drift scope** — drift formations that push off-screen wrap
  at the entity level; formation *bases* and shaping logic stay as-is.
- **Scope-creep guard** — seam-aware spread/radial patterns (Q2 option b) are
  out of scope; if wanted later they are tracked as a new work item, not added
  here. Any extra archetype exclusion discovered during planning becomes a new
  work item or is documented as a divergence, not silent scope growth.
- **Assumption: config plumbing** — the parameter lives in `EnemyConfig`
  (CSV-backed, editor-editable), consistent with the established data-driven
  enemy tooling; default `true` for all archetypes except the explicit
  exclusions.

## Related work

- **AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0** — "Bullets should have a distance and should wrap
  around the screen" (completed). Bullets already wrap; this item builds
  directly on that model for launch direction.
- **AH-0MV8BSMXC0097KLW** — "Enemies should emerge from the wormhole" (open).
  Touches the same shared enemy spawn/motion seams; potential overlap to watch
  during planning.
- **AH-0MU4KQ6NT006MP52** — "Extract common enemy base class for regular
  enemies" (completed). `BaseEnemy` hosts the shared config/seam support.
- **AH-0MTFP7EIC004F1MN** — "Enemy Design tooling" (completed). The
  data-driven `EnemyConfig` pipeline this parameter extends.
- **AH-0MTAN4X5D009D7U6** — "Write ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md
  best-practice guide" (completed). The doc updated by AC 5.
- **AH-0MUGZDTFX004RBD1** — gym↔game parity convention (referenced in
  `AGENTS.md`), enforced by `CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts`.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Movement scope: which enemies should actually 'fly over the edge'? (a)
  All wrap-aware archetypes — shared post-motion wrap in scene loops;
  march/centipede excluded. (b) Firing only. (c) A curated subset."
  — Answer (Map): "(a)". Source: interactive reply, intake round 1.
- Q2: "Firing scope: which fire patterns become seam-aware? (a) Aimed shots
  only. (b) All patterns."
  — Answer (Map): "(a)". Source: interactive reply, intake round 1.

# Audio Design Chapter — retro-arcade survival game GDD

## Problem statement

The GDD currently defines only SFX (§7.3 Audio Direction) and states background music is out of MVP scope with no musical direction defined. The game lacks a documented musical identity (scales, motifs, harmonic language, instrumentation, dynamic mixing, and state-driven music architecture) to guide composition and implementation when music is eventually built.

## Users

- **Audio designers and composers** — need a definitive musical language (scales/modes, motifs, progressions, instrumentation palette) to write consistent, on-brief music.
- **Technical audio programmers** — need the implementation contract (bus architecture, priority tiers, ducking, state machine, middleware guidance) to build or integrate the music system.
- **Game designers / producers** — need per-game-state emotional targets and transition rules to keep audio aligned with gameplay pacing.

User stories:

- As an audio designer, I want documented scales and motifs per game state, so my compositions match the game's emotional arc without guesswork.
- As a technical audio programmer, I want the music state machine and dynamic-mixing rules defined, so I can implement or configure the music engine against a fixed contract.
- As a producer, I want music explicitly scoped as design reference (out of MVP), so the shipped SFX scope (§7.3) is not disturbed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — New chapter file created:** An **AI Hell Music System** chapter is saved as a Markdown GDD addendum at `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`. Its **musical substance** is taken from the producer's original *Music & Thematic Audio Design* brief (Phrygian Dominant + Lydian scales; Combat Motifs A and B and the ambient "Star Drift" motif; the combat, boss and ambient progressions; the FM 2–4 operator + chiptune implementation notes — reproduced under **Source material (A)** below) and laid out in the **8-section + 2-appendix** professional structure of the approved reference brief (Ross, v1.0, 16 October 2026): **1** Audio Vision Statement; **2** Musical Identity (2.1 Tonal Language, 2.2 Core Motifs, 2.3 Chord Progressions); **3** Instrumentation Palette; **4** Dynamic Mixing Rules; **5** State-Driven Music Transitions (5.1 Transition Design Principles, 5.2 Transition Matrix, 5.3 Stinger System); **6** Implementation Guidelines (6.1 Audio Middleware, 6.2 Music Event Architecture, 6.3 Parameter Mapping Table, 6.4 Technical Specifications, 6.5 Audio Budget Table); **7** Composer and Sound Designer Briefs (7.1 Composer Brief, 7.2 Sound Designer Brief); **8** Audio Accessibility; **Appendix A** Motif Reference Sheet; **Appendix B** Glossary. The reference brief is a **structure exemplar only** — its Tableau card-game substance (D Dorian, harpsichord/cello ensemble, card-table SFX, parlour ambience) must **not** be imported into AI Hell's chapter.
- [ ] **AC2 — GDD §7.3 references the chapter:** The "Background Music" subsection in GDD §7.3 (Audio Direction) is updated to link the new chapter file, while retaining the explicit statement that background music is **out of MVP scope** (design reference only; SFX remains the only in-scope audio).
- [ ] **AC3 — GDD §8 future-scope row updated:** The "Background music" row in §8 (Future Scope) references the new chapter file so the doc stays self-consistent.
- [ ] **AC4 — Doc-only change, no behaviour impact:** No game code, SFX behaviour, or runtime audio pipeline is changed; existing §7.3 SFX scope and the shipped ToneForge pipeline remain authoritative for the MVP.
- [ ] **AC5 — Validation:** A new docs guard `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention, e.g. `src/powerUpWeaponRosterDocs.test.ts`) asserts, and passes, that: (i) `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` exists; (ii) it carries all 8 numbered sections plus Appendix A and Appendix B of the approved reference structure; (iii) GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection links the chapter **and** still states music is out of MVP scope; (iv) the GDD §8 "Background music" row links the chapter. All links resolve, and any index/table-of-contents entries are updated.
- [ ] **AC6 — Full project test suite must pass with the new changes** (docs-only; confirms no accidental code impact).

## Constraints

- Music remains **"design reference, out of MVP scope"** — no change to the existing scope stance in GDD §7.3 or §8.
- The chapter is a **synthesis**, not a verbatim import (Q4/Q5, this session): the **musical content** is the producer's original retro-arcade brief reproduced faithfully (Source material (A)); the **document structure** follows the approved reference brief (author: Ross; version 1.0; dated 16 October 2026 — Source material (B)). The reference brief's Tableau card-game substance is **not** carried over.
- Follow the repo's docs naming/style conventions where sensible (singular Markdown addendum under `docs/`, referenced by relative link).
- UK English throughout.

## Existing state

- GDD §7.3 "Audio Direction" covers MVP SFX: baked ToneForge WAV pipeline, SFX event catalogue, per-enemy/per-player audio character, beat-synced explosion accents, and a one-paragraph "Background Music" subsection stating music is a nice-to-have, out of MVP.
- GDD §8 "Future Scope" lists "Background music — Synthwave / retro electronic soundtrack" with no further detail.
- No existing work item implements or specifies background music; the work log contains no musical-identity design doc.

## Desired change

- Add the Audio Design Chapter (AI Hell musical content in the approved reference structure) as a standalone GDD addendum document.
- Point GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection and §8's future-scope row at the new document.
- Keep all gameplay/SFX/runtime behaviour untouched.

**Key Files:**
- `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` (new) — the Audio Design Chapter addendum (confirm filename at implementation)
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §7.3 "Background Music" subsection updated with a link + scope note; §8 "Background music" row updated with a link
- `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (new) — docs guard following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention
- `./README.md` (if it indexes docs) — optional link to the new chapter

## Related work

- **Update GDD audio design section and code comments (AH-0MTGS9DZ6001IFJR)** — completed; historical GDD §7.3 SFX additions, unrelated to music direction.
- **Update audio documentation (AH-0MUTYV9QV0000HDT)** — completed; ToneForge baked-asset pipeline docs; source of the current §7.3 scope language.
- **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — this item.
- See also GDD §7.3 and §8, and `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md` for the authoritative SFX cue catalogue.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Scope-stance divergence (medium):** the chapter is "APPROVED FOR PRODUCTION" in tone while the GDD keeps music out of MVP. Mitigated by AC2/AC3 explicitly framing the chapter as design reference; implementation remains a future work item.
- **Middleware references (FMOD/Wwise) are forward-looking:** the game currently uses Phaser/Web Audio with baked assets (§7.3). The chapter's §9 middleware guidance is design intent for future integration, not an instruction to adopt FMOD/Wwise in the MVP. Noted in the chapter context if needed.
- **Content divergence from shipped SFX:** the chapter (§6.4) proposes procedural SFX recipes that differ from the shipped baked-ToneForge SFX catalogue. The chapter is an addendum; §7.3 remains authoritative for MVP SFX (per constraint). Recorded as an assumption.
- **Scope creep:** producer may later want chapter sections mapped into the live audio system — that is future implementation work, tracked separately, not part of this docs-only item.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Where in the GDD should the 'Music & Thematic Audio Design' content live? (a) replace the §7.3 'Background Music' paragraph with the full chapter; (b) keep the paragraph and add a new top-level section; (c) other." — Answer (user): "A — below is a full brief for the music. Use this to create a new file and refer to it from 7.3." Source: interactive reply. The final decision refines (a): rather than inlining, create a **new file** (`docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`) and **refer to it from GDD §7.3**; adopted as AC1/AC2.
- Q2: "MVP scope statement for music — (a) keep music 'design reference, out of MVP scope'; (b) promote into MVP." — Answer (user): "A." Source: interactive reply. Adopted as the chapter's scope framing (AC2/AC3).
- Q3: "§8 Future Scope 'Background music' row — (a) update to reference the new chapter; (b) leave untouched." — Answer (user): "A." Source: interactive reply. Adopted as AC3.

### Plan-session clarifications (2026-10-23)

- Q4: "What should `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` actually contain? (a) author an AI Hell Music System chapter from the producer's *original retro-arcade* content (Phrygian Dominant + Lydian, Combat Motifs A/B & Star Drift, progressions, FM 2–4 op + chiptune notes) laid out in the approved reference brief's professional structure — the reference brief serving as format exemplar only; (b) import the reference brief verbatim as-is; (c) adapt the reference brief's content to AI Hell's palette; (d) freeform." — Answer (producer): "**1. a**". Source: interactive reply, this plan session. Research: the reference brief describes **Tableau**, a candlelit card game (D Dorian, harpsichord, cello, FMOD, card-table SFX) and is therefore not AI Hell's musical content — AI Hell is a retro-arcade bullet-hell (GDD §1: inspirations Galaxians/classic arcade shoot-'em-ups). The intake session on 2026-10-16 flagged this same conflict and the question was never answered, which left AC1 unverifiable until now. Adopted as the corrected **AC1**.
- Q5: "AC1 enumerates ten sections including *Recommended Scales & Modes* and *Playtesting & Iteration*, but the approved reference brief actually has eight numbered sections plus two appendices and contains no *Playtesting & Iteration* section. (a) correct AC1 to the brief's real structure; (b) keep the ten-section enumeration and build the chapter to it." — Answer (producer): "**2. a**". Source: interactive reply, this plan session. Evidence: reference brief table of contents (Source material (B)). Adopted as the corrected **AC1**.
- Q6: "The full source brief is not embedded in the work item (only section names are), so an implementer cannot reproduce content faithfully and AC1's verbatim requirement is unverifiable. (a) recover the full text from the 2026-10-16 intake session log and embed it in the work item; (b) producer re-supplies the brief." — Answer (producer): "**3. a**". Source: interactive reply, this plan session. Evidence: recovered from session log `~/.pi/agent/sessions/--home-rgardler-projects-AI_Hell--/2026-10-16T11-00-00-344Z_herdr-1792148399-1716826-22311.jsonl`. Adopted as **Source material (A)** below plus the reference-brief record held in this item's comments.
- Q7: Producer additionally instructed: "Also create a follow up work item to implement the design." — Answer (producer): directive recorded verbatim. Source: interactive reply, this plan session. Adopted as follow-up implementation work item **Build the music system from the Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** tracked separately (dependency: the implementation is blocked by this docs item), consistent with the *Scope creep* risk entry and the out-of-MVP scope stance (AC2/AC3).

### Source material (A) — producer's original *Music & Thematic Audio Design* brief (verbatim)

This is the authoritative **musical content** for the new chapter. Reproduced verbatim from the producer's original prompt (2026-10-16). UK-English and retro-arcade framing must be preserved; formatting artefacts in the original (runs such as `♭7Example (E)`) may be repaired into readable Markdown without changing substance.

```markdown
Music & Thematic Audio Design

This section defines the musical identity of the game, focusing on scales, motifs, harmonic language, and usage guidelines across gameplay states. The goal is to merge retro‑arcade space tension (Asteroids) with relentless survival energy (Vampire Survivors), using a coherent musical palette that supports procedural layering and dynamic intensity shifts.

🎼 1. Core Musical Identity

The soundtrack is built around two complementary scales:

Primary Combat Scale — Phrygian Dominant

Used for: wave combat, boss spawns, high‑intensity survival phases.

Scale Formula: 1 ♭2 3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7Example (E): E – F – G♯ – A – B – C – D

Why:

Retro‑arcade tension

Exotic, driving, instantly “space danger”

Works extremely well with FM bass, square leads, and arpeggiators

Provides strong melodic hooks with minimal notes

Secondary Ambient Scale — Lydian

Used for: menus, starfield travel, upgrade screens, low‑intensity exploration.

Scale Formula: 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7Example (C): C – D – E – F♯ – G – A – B

Why:

Bright, floating, cosmic

Contrasts the combat scale without breaking aesthetic cohesion

Ideal for pads, shimmering arps, and soft synth textures

🎵 2. Melodic Motifs

Motifs are intentionally short (2–6 notes) to support looping, procedural recombination, and chiptune‑style repetition.

Combat Motif A — “Incoming Wave”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Contour: Rising tension → abrupt dropNotes: E – F – G♯ – F – E – DUsage:

Triggered at the start of each enemy wave

Can be fragmented into E–F–G♯ for micro‑stingers

Works well as a 3‑note arpeggiated alert

Combat Motif B — “Survival Pulse”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Rhythmic Cell: Dotted + straightNotes: G♯ – A – G♯ – F – EUsage:

Mid‑combat loop

Easily reharmonized for intensity scaling

Can be doubled with FM bass for crunchy retro drive

Ambient Motif — “Star Drift”

Scale: Lydian (C)Contour: Floating, circularNotes: C – E – F♯ – E – D – CUsage:

Menu screens

Upgrade/shop interface

Slow arpeggiated background texture

🎹 3. Harmonic Progressions

Retro arcade music often avoids complex harmony, but these progressions provide structure while staying loop‑friendly.

Combat Progression (Phrygian Dominant)

E – F – E – D

Minimalist, modal, tense

Works with pulsing bass and rapid arps

Can be expanded to E – F – G♯ – F – E – D – C – D for boss phases

Boss Progression (Phrygian Dominant, extended)

E – C – D – F – E

Chromatic tension

Strong “danger escalation” feel

Supports heavy FM brass or distorted square leads

Ambient Progression (Lydian)

C – D – E – F♯

Bright, drifting, spacey

Works well with pads and slow-moving textures

Can be looped seamlessly or expanded to C – G – D – F♯

🔧 4. Implementation Notes

Motifs should be stored as atomic musical objects (interval sets + rhythm cells) for procedural recombination.

Combat layers should increase harmonic density (more voices, faster arps) rather than changing the motif.

Ambient layers should use long‑release envelopes and minimal rhythmic content.

FM synthesis (2–4 operators) and chiptune waveforms (square, triangle, noise) define the retro palette.

All motifs should be designed to loop cleanly at 1–2 bars for dynamic layering.
```

### Source material (B) — approved reference brief (structure exemplar)

The full 58 KB reference document (Ross, v1.0, 16 October 2026) that defines the **chapter structure** is recorded verbatim in a comment on this work item titled *Source material (B) — approved reference brief (structure exemplar), verbatim*. It describes the card game **Tableau**; treat its **section architecture, table layouts, parameter/stinger/matrix formats and glossary style** as the template, and its **musical and SFX substance as out of scope**.

## Verification approach

Docs-only change, but the repo convention is that cross-cutting docs slices ship with a `*Docs.test.ts` guard
(12 sibling guards exist, e.g. `src/powerUpWeaponRosterDocs.test.ts`, `src/enemyRosterDocs.test.ts`). The guard
for this item asserts file existence, the reference-brief section structure, and both GDD cross-links —
including the "out of MVP scope" sentence, so a future edit cannot silently promote music into the MVP.

Manual checks that complement the guard:
- Open `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` and confirm every Source material (A) element maps into the document
  (two scales, three motifs, three progressions, four implementation notes) — nothing dropped, nothing invented.
- Confirm no Tableau substance leaked in (no D Dorian as the home mode, no harpsichord/cello ensemble, no
  card-table SFX).
- Confirm §7.3's SFX catalogue, autoplay and rate-limiting text is untouched (AC4).

AC6 is satisfied by the standard dev-push gate (full suite); the guard above gives the changed-scope signal.

## Related work (automated report)

### Related work items
- **AH-0MT7UW0Y80062NU1** – Bring simple audio effects into MVP scope in GDD (interactions, impacts, enemy actions, advanced telegraphing) (completed)
- **AH-0MUTYV9QV0000HDT** – Update audio documentation (completed)
- **AH-0MTGS9DZ6001IFJR** – Update GDD audio design section and code comments (completed)

### Repository file matches
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — matched: audio, design, gdd, music, update
- `CHANGELOG.md` — matched: audio, design, music, update
- `README.md` — matched: audio, design, gdd, update

Follow-up to Scripted Gameplay Videos (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC), discovered-from:AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC.

When the producer resolved the intake scene-target question as **"A now, C later"**, this item records the deferred Option C: extend multi-scene scripted capture so a scene target can be a **freshly generated shipped-game level** (the literal brief: "create a level, play it for x seconds, capture y seconds"), rather than only dev gym scene keys.

## Problem statement
Option A (gym scene keys) gives showcase variety quickly but uses dev-only scenes rather than the shipped game. Option C records real procedurally-generated PlayScene levels, which is the literal intent of the original brief and better marketing material, but needs more work (a dev-gated in-place "start a fresh level" hook plus a multi-wave-aware capture window).

## User story
As the maintainer, I can capture several freshly generated game levels in one compiled video so a promo shows real, varied shipped gameplay rather than dev gyms.

## Acceptance Criteria (indicative — refine at intake)
- A JSON scene entry can target a generated game level (e.g. optional seed/level index), reusing the Option A capture-director plumbing.
- Switching to a new generated level happens page-side without a page reload, so the single MediaRecorder keeps rolling.
- Multi-wave play/capture window handling avoids recording quiet gaps (e.g. per-scene capture driven by wave/action signals).
- Single stitched WebM output with 0.25 s fades, consistent with Option A.
- All related documentation updated; full project test suite passes.

## Notes
- Depends on the Option A capture-director foundation delivered by AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC.
- Related (not a blocker): Compile an action video (AH-0MV9DB68T002IROX).

# Stream recorder chunks to disk through a bounded sink

Parent: **AH-0MVN06MS9007LRKE** (Capture crashes on long full-run clips).

## Goal / user story

As the person producing a full 30-minute playthrough, I want the capture to
write the recording to disk as it arrives, so node memory stays flat instead of
holding the whole clip (≈1.8 GB at 8 Mbps for 30 min) and a long run cannot OOM
(parent AC2).

## Context

Both capture paths currently accumulate every chunk in a node array and
`Buffer.concat` once at the end:
`scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs:1456-1458` (single/batch clip) and `:1899-1901`
(`--scenes`), concatenated at `:1598` and `:2024`. Replace that array with a
shared, tested sink that appends each decoded chunk to the output file
immediately.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A new shared sink module appends each base64 chunk to the output file as it
   arrives (decode → write), so peak node memory is O(one chunk) rather than
   O(run duration); no whole-run buffer is ever built.
2. The sink reports `bytesWritten`, `chunkCount` and `peakPendingBytes`, and no
   single retained in-memory buffer exceeds the configured chunk cap.
3. A hermetic unit test drives the sink with simulated chunks whose cumulative
   total exceeds the 512 MB CDP pipe budget (written to a temp file, so the
   bound is proven without a 30-minute soak) and asserts: on-disk bytes equal
   the sum of the chunk sizes, `peakPendingBytes` never exceeds one chunk,
   nothing is retained after each write, and the sink is idempotent across
   repeated runs (fresh temp dir per test).
4. The chunk cap / prefix-budget constants are declared once (single-sourced
   next to `DEFAULT_MAX_CAPTURE_DURATION_MS` in
   `scripts/capture-run-lifecycle.mjs`) and imported by the sink, the page-side
   guard and the probe.
5. The sink writes to a temporary `.partial` path and finalises (rename) only
   when the caller reports success — the rename policy itself is exercised in
   the salvage item, but the sink must expose the seam.
6. Existing capture tests keep passing unmodified; no new runtime dependency.

## Key Files

- `scripts/capture-chunk-sink.mjs` (**new**) + `capture-chunk-sink.d.mts`
  (**new**).
- `scripts/capture-chunk-sink.test.ts` (**new**) — or the sink cases appended to
  `scripts/capture-gameplay.test.ts`; pick whichever the repo's test layout
  prefers and keep it hermetic (`@vitest-environment node`).
- `scripts/capture-run-lifecycle.mjs` — shared chunk-cap/prefix constants.
- `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` — consume the sink (both call sites).

## Notes

- TDD: write the failing sink tests first (they are the AC2 proof), then the
  module.
- The sink must not buffer in the calling code either: after each write the
  decoded buffer must be droppable.
data.title: Stream recorder chunks to disk through a bounded sink

# Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture

## Problem statement

Multi-scene capture (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC) records several gym scenes into one WebM, driven by a `scenes.json` list. Today a scene entry can only name a `target` key plus `playMs` / `captureMs` / `label`; the scene's **content** is hard-coded by the scene class. Consequences:

- `GymLevel` always starts the player with spread + dual permanently equipped and plays whatever `LevelDefinition` launched it — but nothing in the capture path can supply one.
- `GymFodderEnemies` needs an `enemyKey` and cannot be started from a key at all.
- Both parameterised scenes are therefore excluded from `WATCHABLE_GYM_SCENE_KEYS` (`unsupported-target`), and the in-page director's `start(key)` accepts no launch data.
- Formation gyms (`GymBoss`, `GymCentipede`, `GymMiniBoss`, …) have fixed rosters and loadouts, so a showcase cannot show "the player with shield level 2 and the rapid weapon, on level 4 wave 2, fighting these enemies".

The recording machinery already supports everything needed except the data: `scene.start(key, data)` is how gyms are launched everywhere else, `LevelDefinition` / `WaveDefinition` are plain serialisable data, `Player.equipWeapon(id, permanent)` and `PowerUpLevelStore.collect(id, permanent)` are the shared loadout seams, and seeded RNG (`createSeededRng` / `normaliseSeed`) is already used by `GymBotTuning`.

## User stories

- As the maintainer, I can describe a scene's setup (level, waves, enemies, player weapons and power-ups, RNG seed) inside `scenes.json`, so one config produces exactly the gameplay a video needs.
- As the maintainer, I can re-run the same config and get the same recording, so a clip can be re-cut, compared or regenerated after a balance change.
- As a reviewer, a bad setup is rejected **before** the browser boots with an actionable error, instead of recording a blank or unintended scene.
- As an implementer, setups are applied through the same shared seams the shipped game uses, so gym↔game parity (and the duplicate-body guard) is preserved rather than forked.

## Expected behaviour

A scene entry gains an optional `setup` object. Absent `setup` ⇒ today's behaviour, byte-for-byte unchanged. Present ⇒ validated before boot, normalised with documented defaults, passed through the dev-only director into the target scene's `init`, and applied **during the warm-up (`playMs`) window** so the first captured frame already shows the configured state.

Illustrative shape (final field names fixed by C1):

```json
{
  "scenes": [
    {
      "target": "GymLevel",
      "playMs": 2000,
      "captureMs": 4000,
      "label": "level 4, wave 2, shield 2",
      "setup": {
        "seed": 42,
        "level": {
          "level": 4,
          "name": "The Core",
          "waves": [
            { "groups": [{ "enemyKey": "scout", "formation": "grid", "count": 6 }],
              "shootEnabled": true }
          ]
        },
        "startWave": 2,
        "player": { "weapons": ["spread", "dual", "rapid"] },
        "powerUps": { "shield": 2, "smart_bomb": 1 }
      }
    },
    {
      "target": "GymFodderEnemies",
      "playMs": 1500,
      "captureMs": 2500,
      "setup": { "enemy": "grunt", "player": { "weapons": ["spread"] } }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Setup schema and defaults.** A scene entry accepts an optional `setup` object covering at minimum: a `LevelDefinition`-shaped level (`level`, `name`, `waves[]` with `groups[]` and the existing opt-in flags), a starting wave index, the enemy key(s) that select a formation-gym roster, the player loadout (permanent + timed weapon ids, power-up levels), and a `seed`. Every field has a documented default; an entry without `setup` behaves exactly as today (proved by an unchanged-behaviour test).
- **AC2 — Fail-fast validation.** Invalid setups are rejected with `Scene config error: …` and exit 1 **before** any Vite server or browser boots. New stable error codes cover at least: unknown/invalid field, unknown `enemyKey`, unknown formation kind, unknown weapon id, unknown power-up id, non-positive/out-of-range level or wave index, missing required setup for a parameterised target, and a setup supplied to a target that cannot accept it. Codes are asserted in tests rather than on message wording, mirroring the existing `SCENE_CONFIG_ERROR_CODES` pattern.
- **AC3 — Director passes setup through.** The dev-only in-page director exposes `start(key, setup?)` and forwards the setup as `scene.start(key, setup)`, keeping one page and one continuously running `MediaRecorder` (no navigation or reload). `GymLevel` and `GymFodderEnemies` become recordable **when** the setup supplies their required parameter, and remain rejected with a clear `unsupported-target`-class error when it does not. Validation stays shared between CLI and director (single source of truth), and the registry pinning test is updated so the watchable set and the gym files on disk cannot drift.
- **AC4 — Shared setup application, no forked gameplay.** One shared, unit-tested helper applies a normalised setup to a scene's existing seams (`LevelDefinition` hand-off, `Player.equipWeapon`, `PowerUpLevelStore.collect`) inside `init`/`create` before the first captured frame. **No scene-class generation and no duplicated gameplay bodies** — the gym↔game parity convention (AGENTS.md; `CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts` duplicate-body guard) stays green, and the helper is the only place that knows how a setup becomes play state.
- **AC5 — Determinism.** Setup-driven randomness (enemy/formation placement, drop cadence, any generated content) is seeded from the config, so the same config yields the same scene content run to run; the resolved seed is reported in the `--json` payload. A test asserts identical derived state for two runs of the same seed and different state for different seeds.
- **AC6 — Machine-readable reporting.** The `--json` payload reports, per scene, the **normalised** setup actually applied (defaults filled in) alongside the existing `target` / `playMs` / `captureMs` / `startMs` / `endMs`, so a consumer can reproduce the recording without re-deriving defaults.
- **AC7 — Documentation, examples and gates.** `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` documents the `setup` schema, defaults, error codes and a worked example; `README.md` and `examples/scenes.json` are updated with a setup-bearing example. Hermetic tests cover schema validation, defaults, normalisation, determinism and director pass-through; the full project suite (`/skill:test`), `npm run build` and `npm run check-bundle` all pass.

## Constraints

- **No scene-code generation.** "Scene generator" means a *parametriser* producing launch data for existing shared scenes. Emitting bespoke scene classes would fork the gameplay path and violate the gym↔game parity rule.
- **Dev-only and bundle-inert.** Director and `src/` plumbing stay behind `import.meta.env.DEV`; `npm run check-bundle` must stay green.
- **One recorder, one page.** Scene switching stays in-page; no navigation or reload.
- **WebM only.** No transcoding (no VP9 ffmpeg available).
- **Backward compatible.** Every existing `scenes.json` (including `examples/scenes.json`) keeps working untouched.

## Out of scope

- Generated shipped-game `PlayScene` levels (the "Option C" target) — tracked by AH-0MVE01EY0008QEVX, which this epic unblocks by supplying the setup pass-through.
- Runtime (in-UI) editing of scene setups; setups are file-defined only.
- Any change to the shipped game's balance, catalogues or rules.

## Assumptions (recorded, to be confirmed in C1)

- `LevelDefinition` / `WaveDefinition` / `WaveGroup` (`src/waves/Formations.ts`) are already fully serialisable and sufficient to express "the enemies to appear, the level and wave numbers".
- `Player.equipWeapon(id, permanent)` and `Player.getPowerUpLevelStore().collect(id, permanent)` are the correct shared loadout seams; power-up ids self-validate via `getPowerUpById`.
- `applyEnemyCountScaling` means a configured group `count` is a *base* count that level scaling then transforms — the schema must state whether configured counts are pre- or post-scaling.
- Seeding the shared RNG for the duration of a capture is sufficient for reproducibility; audio-visual jitter outside RNG (frame timing) is acceptable.

## Existing state / key files (predicted)

- `scripts/capture-scenes.mjs` — pure multi-scene core: `parseSceneConfig`, `loadSceneConfig`, `buildScenePlan`, `SCENE_CONFIG_ERROR_CODES`, `WATCHABLE_GYM_SCENE_KEYS`, `PARAMETERISED_GYM_SCENE_KEYS`, payload builder.
- `scripts/capture-scenes.test.ts` / `.d.mts` — hermetic contract tests and types; registry pinned against `src/scenes/gym/` on disk.
- `src/core/captureDirector.ts` — dev-gated `window.__aiHellCaptureDirector.start(key)`; `resolveSceneKey` validates against the shared registry plus page discovery.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymLevel.ts` — already accepts `{ waves, levelName }` / `{ level }`; hard-codes spread+dual at start.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymFodderEnemies.ts` — `init({ enemyKey })`; resolves config via `loadEnemyConfig`.
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts` — shared base for the formation gyms (roster/loadout seams).
- `src/waves/Formations.ts` — `LevelDefinition`, `WaveDefinition`, `WaveGroup`, `LEVELS`.
- `src/entities/Player.ts` — `equipWeapon`, `resetWeapon`, `getPowerUpLevelStore`.
- `src/powerups/powerUpLevels.ts` — `PowerUpLevelStore.collect`.
- `src/core/rng.ts` — `createSeededRng`, `normaliseSeed`, `randomSeed`.
- `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` — `--scenes` mode: boot, recorder, fade overlay, probes, `--json`.
- `examples/scenes.json`, `README.md`, `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md`, `src/multiSceneCaptureDocs.test.ts`.

## Related work

- **Scripted Gameplay Videos (AH-0MUX2NLFZ00128WC)** — `completed`. The multi-scene capture foundation this extends.
- **Dev-gated in-page capture scene director (AH-0MVFC6WPS004UOLO)** — `completed`. Currently key-only; AC3 extends it.
- **Pure scene-capture module (AH-0MVFC6TCY005E39P)** — `completed`. Where the setup schema and validation land.
- **Scripted Gameplay Videos: generated-level scenes (Option C follow-up) (AH-0MVE01EY0008QEVX)** — `idea`. Blocked by this epic's setup pass-through; dependency edge recorded.
- **Compile an action video (AH-0MV9DB68T002IROX)** — `open`. Consumes captured footage; a setup-bearing capture gives it better material.
data.title: Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture

# C1 — Setup schema, defaults and fail-fast validation (test-first)

Child of Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture (AH-0MVNW7U5G003SNO6). Parent ACs: AC1, AC2 (and AC6 defaults half).

## Summary

Define, in the pure browser-free module `scripts/capture-scenes.mjs`, the `setup` schema a `scenes.json` entry may carry, its documented defaults, its normalisation, and fail-fast validation with stable machine-readable error codes. Tests first (red), then the implementation. No browser, no `src/` changes.

## User story

As the maintainer, a typo (unknown enemy, bad wave index, unknown power-up id) fails in milliseconds with an actionable message naming the offending scene entry and field, instead of booting Chromium and recording the wrong thing.

## Scope

- Extend the parsed scene-entry shape with an optional `setup` object. When absent, the parsed entry and every downstream artefact must be **identical** to today's (add an explicit unchanged-behaviour test).
- Model the setup as: level (`LevelDefinition`-shaped: `level`, `name`, `waves[]` with `groups[]` and the existing opt-in flags `shootEnabled` / `ghosts` / `centipede` / `horde` / `laneTraffic` / `miniBoss`), a starting wave index, an enemy key for formation gyms, the player loadout (permanent and timed weapon ids), power-up levels by id, and a `seed`.
- Normalisation fills documented defaults (e.g. default weapon set when `player` is omitted, default seed, default starting wave) and drops nothing silently.
- Validation rejects, with new codes in `SCENE_CONFIG_ERROR_CODES`: unknown field, wrong type, unknown `enemyKey`, unknown formation kind, unknown weapon id, unknown power-up id, level/wave index out of range, missing required parameter for a parameterised target (`GymLevel` / `GymFodderEnemies`), and a setup supplied to a target that cannot accept one.

## Acceptance criteria

- Tests exist **first** and cover: absent-setup unchanged behaviour; each new error code; defaults filled by normalisation; idempotent normalisation (normalise(normalise(x)) deep-equals normalise(x)); setup preserved per entry in file order alongside the existing timing fields.
- Error messages name the scene index and field; codes (not wording) are asserted.
- The module still imports nothing (no Node APIs, no DOM, no Vite) so both the CLI and the in-page director can import it.
- Types are extended in `scripts/capture-scenes.d.mts` and typecheck cleanly.
- The existing registry-pinning test and `src/multiSceneCaptureDocs.test.ts` still pass.

## Key Files

- `scripts/capture-scenes.mjs`
- `scripts/capture-scenes.test.ts`
- `scripts/capture-scenes.d.mts`
- `src/core/captureDirector.ts` (consumer; read-only here)
- `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` (error-code table; prose lands in C5)

## Minimal implementation

Add `parseSceneSetup` / `normaliseSceneSetup` / `validateSceneSetup` pure functions and a `SCENE_SETUP_FIELD_SPECS` style table, mirroring the existing `parseSceneConfig` structure and error-code discipline. Valid ids are resolved from the existing shared registries (`loadEnemyConfig` keys, `WeaponId`, `getPowerUpById`) via dependency injection or a frozen mirrored list with a parity test — do **not** hand-copy a drifting list.

## Dependencies

None (first item). Everything else consumes this contract.

## Deliverables

Schema + defaults + validation + types + tests, all hermetic.

# C2 — Director and registry: pass setup through `start(key, setup)`

Child of Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture (AH-0MVNW7U5G003SNO6). Parent ACs: AC3.

## Summary

Make the dev-only in-page capture director accept launch data and forward it into the target scene, and gate the previously rejected parameterised gyms on the presence of a valid setup — so `GymLevel` and `GymFodderEnemies` become recordable without any page navigation.

## User story

As the maintainer, I can record `GymLevel` and `GymFodderEnemies` in a multi-scene capture by supplying their setup in `scenes.json`, and the single `MediaRecorder` keeps rolling across the switch.

## Scope

- `start(key, setup?)` forwards the (already normalised) setup as `scene.start(key, setup)` through the existing scene-manager path.
- `resolveSceneKey` / `startScene` gating: a key in `PARAMETERISED_GYM_SCENE_KEYS` is accepted **only** with a setup that satisfies its required parameter, and rejected otherwise with the shared error code. Non-parameterised keys keep today's behaviour; an unexpected setup on a target that cannot consume it is rejected consistently with C1.
- Update `WATCHABLE_GYM_SCENE_KEYS` semantics (or introduce the accessor that resolves "watchable given this setup") so the CLI pre-boot validation and the director guard stay a single source of truth, and the registry pinning test against `src/scenes/gym/` on disk is updated deliberately.
- Capture driver (`scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` `--scenes` mode) passes each entry's setup to the director call and reports the normalised setup in the `--json` payload (AC6).

## Acceptance criteria

- A test proves `start(key, setup)` reaches the scene manager as `start(key, <normalised setup>)` and that no navigation/reload occurs (director fake, no browser).
- `GymLevel` without setup ⇒ rejected; with a valid setup ⇒ accepted. Same for `GymFodderEnemies` (`enemy` key). Both assertions made for **both** the CLI validation path and the director path, so the two can never disagree.
- The registry/deviation is documented in code comments, and the pinning test fails if a gym scene is added or removed without updating the registry.
- Dev gate unchanged: `isCaptureDirectorEnabled()` is constant `false` in a production build and `npm run check-bundle` stays green.
- The `--json` payload exposes, per scene, the normalised setup alongside the existing timing fields.

## Key Files

- `src/core/captureDirector.ts`
- `src/core/captureDirector.test.ts`
- `scripts/capture-scenes.mjs` (registry/validation accessors)
- `scripts/capture-scenes.test.ts`
- `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` (`--scenes` mode wiring + payload)
- `scripts/capture-gameplay.test.ts`

## Minimal implementation

Thread a `setup` argument through `startScene` → `SceneManagerLike.start(key, setup)`; add a `resolveWatchableSceneEntry(entry)` that returns the resolved key plus normalised setup, used by both the CLI's pre-boot loop and the director. Keep the existing structural `SceneManagerLike` interfaces so tests stay browser-free.

## Dependencies

- C1 — setup schema, defaults and validation.

## Deliverables

Director pass-through + gated registry + CLI wiring + payload field + hermetic tests.

# C3 — Shared setup application helper and gym integration

Child of Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture (AH-0MVNW7U5G003SNO6). Parent ACs: AC4 (and the loadout/level half of AC1).

## Summary

Add one shared helper that turns a normalised setup into play state using only existing shared seams, and wire it into the gym scenes' `init`/`create` so the configured state is live **before** the first captured frame (i.e. during the `playMs` warm-up).

## User story

As a viewer of a showcase clip, the very first frame of each scene already shows the configured loadout and the configured enemies — no dead frames while a scene "catches up".

## Scope

- New shared helper (suggested `src/scenes/core/sceneSetup.ts`) with a pure-ish `applySceneSetup(scene seams, setup)` entry point:
  - level hand-off: supply the `LevelDefinition` and starting wave to the wave loop (`GymLevel`'s documented `{ level }` / `{ waves, levelName }` launch contract);
  - player loadout: `equipWeapon(id, true)` for configured permanent weapons, `equipWeapon(id, false)` + timer for configured timed weapons, and `PowerUpLevelStore.collect(id, permanent)` for configured power-up levels;
  - formation-gym enemy selection: the `enemyKey` seam `GymFodderEnemies.init` already uses, generalised to the formation gyms that can accept it.
- Wire it into `GymLevel`, `GymFodderEnemies` and `GymFormationScene`-derived gyms at the earliest safe point (before wave scheduling and before the supply layer's first tick), preserving current behaviour when no setup is supplied.
- Replace `GymLevel`'s hard-coded spread+dual with a **default** that the helper reproduces exactly, so today's behaviour is unchanged when `player` is omitted.
- Keep the helper the *only* place that knows how a setup becomes play state (no per-scene copies of the mapping).

## Acceptance criteria

- A test asserts the same state after applying a setup: expected active weapon ids (`getActiveWeapons`), weapon levels, power-up effective levels, and the launched wave list for a configured level + starting wave.
- With no setup, `GymLevel` / `GymFodderEnemies` / formation gyms produce exactly their pre-change state (explicit unchanged-behaviour test per scene touched).
- Setup is applied before the first recorded frame: an integration test drives the warm-up then asserts the captured-window start state matches the setup (no first-frame blank/dead state).
- **Parity preserved:** `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts` duplicate-body guard stays green; the helper contains no gameplay logic that is duplicated from `PlayScene`.
- Any intentional divergence (e.g. a gym that cannot accept a level because it has no campaign-level input, which `GymLevel`'s header already documents for `GymFormationScene`) is recorded in the work item and in a code comment next to the divergence.
- Typecheck, build and the changed-scope tests pass.

## Key Files

- `src/scenes/core/sceneSetup.ts` (new) + `.test.ts`
- `src/scenes/gym/GymLevel.ts`
- `src/scenes/gym/GymFodderEnemies.ts`
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts`
- `src/scenes/gym/GymLevel.test.ts`, `GymFodderEnemies.test.ts`
- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts` (guard must stay green)
- `src/entities/Player.ts`, `src/powerups/powerUpLevels.ts` (consumed, not changed)
- `src/waves/Formations.ts` (consumed, not changed)

## Minimal implementation

One function taking narrow structural seams (`getPlayer()`, `equipWeapon`, wave-queue hand-off) so it is unit-testable with fakes and identical in gyms and (later) other scenes. Explicitly **no** scene-class generation.

## Dependencies

- C1 — setup schema, defaults and validation.

## Deliverables

Shared applier + gym wiring + unchanged-behaviour and applied-state tests.

# C4 — Seeded determinism contract for setup-driven randomness

Child of Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture (AH-0MVNW7U5G003SNO6). Parent AC: AC5.

## Summary

Make setup-driven randomness reproducible from the config's `seed`, so the same `scenes.json` produces the same scene content on every run, and report the resolved seed in the `--json` payload.

## User story

As the maintainer, I can re-record a clip after a balance change and get the same enemy placement and drop sequence, so the only visible difference is the change I made.

## Scope

- Identify every randomness source that affects a configured scene's *content* (formation placement / start ranges, drop spawner cadence, mineral seeding, generated enemies, any scene-local `Math.random`).
- Route those sources through the existing shared `createSeededRng` / `normaliseSeed` (`src/core/rng.ts`) when a setup supplies a seed (or a documented default seed), without changing behaviour when no setup is supplied.
- Report the resolved seed (explicit or defaulted) in the `--json` payload per scene, and document the reproducibility guarantee **and its limits** (frame-timing/encoder jitter is out of scope; content determinism is in scope).

## Acceptance criteria

- A test asserts two runs with the same seed produce identical derived content (spawn positions, enemy keys/counts, drop sequence), and different seeds produce different content for at least one asserted axis.
- A test asserts that an entry **without** `setup` behaves exactly as today (no RNG re-plumbing side effects).
- No `Math.random` remains on a configured scene's content path (asserted by a scan test or by construction + a comment), and the shared RNG is the single source.
- Resolved seed is present in the `--json` payload and documented in the schema docs (prose in C5).
- Full suite and build green.

## Key Files

- `src/core/rng.ts` (consumed)
- `src/scenes/gym/GymLevel.ts`, `GymFodderEnemies.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts`
- `src/core/captureDirector.ts` (seed hand-off)
- `scripts/capture-scenes.mjs` + `.test.ts` (seed defaulting/normalisation)
- `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` (prose in C5)

## Minimal implementation

Thread the seed through the same setup object C1 normalises and C3 applies; seed at the earliest scene-lifecycle point so every later draw is deterministic. Keep the RNG injectable so tests need no browser.

## Dependencies

- C3 — shared setup application helper and gym integration.

## Deliverables

Seeded content path + seed reporting + determinism tests + limits documented.
data.title: Seeded determinism contract for setup-driven randomness

# C5 — Docs, examples and pinned-test sweep

Child of Config-defined scene setups for scripted gameplay capture (AH-0MVNW7U5G003SNO6). Parent ACs: AC7 (and the documentation half of AC6).

## Summary

Document the `setup` schema end to end, ship a working setup-bearing example config, and close the documentation/pinning gates so the feature cannot drift away from its docs.

## User story

As a maintainer reading the repo, I can learn the whole `setup` vocabulary, its defaults and its error codes from one doc, and copy a config that actually records a configured scene.
